evalDetails.reasoning: The response fully satisfies every rubric criterion: OFFSET is completely removed and replaced with a row-value WHERE clause `(created_at, id) < ($1, $2)` that correctly mirrors the DESC, DESC sort; cursors are opaque base64(url)-encoded JSON carrying both created_at and id (compound cursor); the response shape exactly matches the required {posts, pagination:{hasMore, nextCursor, limit}} with no totalCount/COUNT query; the no-cursor first-page path omits the WHERE filter entirely via a separate query branch; the N+1 LIMIT trick is implemented correctly (fetch limit+1, slice, set hasMore); invalid/malformed cursors are caught and return 400; and the explanation covers offset's O(offset) cost, concurrent insert/delete drift/duplication, and the COUNT query's separate scaling cost. Extras (index recommendation, limit clamping, bigint-safe string IDs, base64url instead of base64) are well-justified and don't violate the spec. Only very minor nitpick: using base64url rather than literally 'base64' as stated, though this is explained and functionally superior for a query-string cursor.

Excellent, fully correct implementation. All hard requirements met: WHERE-based keyset with (created_at, id) row-value comparison, no OFFSET; opaque base64 JSON cursor with version field; response has hasMore/nextCursor/limit and no totalCount; first page correctly omits cursor filter; LIMIT N+1 trick used correctly (fetches limit+1, slices, sets hasMore); ORDER BY preserved exactly as compound DESC, DESC; invalid cursor returns 400 via decode try/catch and shape validation; code is syntactically valid with sensible edge-case handling (limit capped, empty result set implicitly handled since posts.length checks guard nextCursor). Explanation section covers no-OFFSET-scan-cost, no-COUNT, concurrent-write stability, and infinite-scroll fit — hits the concurrent-insert consistency point and O(1)-vs-O(offset) implicitly (deep pages progressively slower) though doesn't state Big-O explicitly. Minor nitpicks: uses created_at (not raw id) which is fine per spec; cursor decode validation is reasonably thorough. No deductions apply (no OFFSET, no raw unencoded IDs). Very minor: could have been slightly more explicit about O(1) vs O(offset) complexity terms, and edge case of empty result set isn't explicitly discussed in prose though code handles it correctly.

Excellent conversion meeting nearly all requirements: no OFFSET anywhere, opaque base64-JSON compound cursor (created_at, id) using string-safe id encoding, correct WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1,$2) tuple comparison matching DESC,DESC order, correct first-page handling (no cursor filter), N+1 LIMIT trick properly implemented, response shape matches spec exactly (hasMore, nextCursor, limit, no totalCount), COUNT query removed, robust invalid-cursor handling (malformed base64/JSON, plus a thoughtful DB-error catch for cursors with wrong-typed id) returning 400. Also adds limit validation (not required but reasonable, though caps at 100 vs spec's implicit 20 default — minor deviation not penalized by rubric). Explanation of benefits (index seek, consistent performance, no anomalies from concurrent inserts, avoids expensive count) is present but brief and doesn't explicitly contrast O(1) vs O(offset) complexity. Code is syntactically valid, uses parameterized queries safely. Minor nitpick: tuple comparison (created_at, id) < ($1,$2) requires matching types/collation and works correctly for DESC,DESC compound sort. Overall very strong, essentially complete implementation.

Excellent conversion meeting nearly all requirements: proper keyset WHERE clause with tuple comparison (created_at, id) < ($1,$2) replacing OFFSET entirely, base64url-encoded opaque cursor via helper functions, correct response shape (posts, hasMore, nextCursor, limit) with no totalCount, correctly omits WHERE filter on first page, N+1 LIMIT trick correctly implemented with slicing, compound cursor preserves DESC,DESC sort order, invalid cursor returns 400, COUNT query removed, and clear explanation of advantages (stability under writes, O(1) vs O(offset) cost, no expensive count, compound key avoiding ties). Minor deductions: uses base64url instead of plain base64 (spec said 'base64-encoded JSON string' generically, so this is a reasonable interpretation but a slight deviation), and edge case of empty result set isn't explicitly discussed though the code handles it fine implicitly. Code is syntactically valid and well-structured.
